## Guided Tutorial 14.2: Writing and Testing the Margin Measures

**Context and objective.** In this tutorial, you will write the measures that answer the managers' questions about margin and discounts, and prove them. You will collect the measures in a table of their own, build the sales measures from simple sums to a ratio with a variable, use CALCULATE to fix a filter and to remove one, and show Furniture's margin by quarter. Finally, you will write a tab of tests in DAX query view that compares the measures with the totals of Chapter 6.

**Prerequisites.** You need Charles River Reports.pbix from Tutorial 14.1, with the sales star and the marked Date table.

**Step-by-step instructions.**

**Step 1. Create a table for the measures.**

a. Choose **Home > Enter data**.
b. Type `Measures` as the table's name, leave the single empty column as it is, and click **Load**.

The Measures table appears in the Data pane with one column, Column1. You will hide that column once the table holds its first measure, and the table will then move to the top of the Data pane.

**Step 2. Write the base measures.** Each measure is a named sum or count of the fact table.

a. Select the **Measures** table in the **Data** pane, and choose **Modeling > New measure**.
b. Type the first definition below in the formula bar, and press Enter.
c. Repeat the two actions for each of the other definitions.
d. Select each new measure, and on the **Measure tools** tab, set its format: the thousands separator and two decimals for amounts, and a whole number for the two counts.
e. Right-click Column1 of the Measures table, and choose **Hide in report view**.

<!-- dax-check: measure -->
```
Revenue = SUM ( SalesInvoiceLine[LineTotal] )
List Amount = SUM ( SalesInvoiceLine[ListAmount] )
Discounts = SUM ( SalesInvoiceLine[DiscountAmount] )
Invoice Lines = COUNTROWS ( SalesInvoiceLine )
Invoices = DISTINCTCOUNT ( SalesInvoiceLine[SalesInvoiceID] )
```

Each line is a separate measure, typed one at a time, and with Column1 hidden the Measures table moves to the top of the Data pane. Invoices counts the distinct SalesInvoiceID values among the lines in the filter context, so it now follows any selection on Item, Customer, or Date.

**Step 3. Write the standard cost and the margin.** Standard cost needs an iterator, because the cost per unit lives on the Item table.

a. Add the measures below to the Measures table, as in Step 2.
b. Format Standard Cost and Gross Margin as amounts, and Margin % as a percentage with two decimals.

<!-- dax-check: measure -->
```
Standard Cost =
SUMX (
    SalesInvoiceLine,
    SalesInvoiceLine[Quantity] * RELATED ( 'Item'[StandardCost] )
)
```

<!-- dax-check: measure -->
```
Gross Margin = [Revenue] - [Standard Cost]
```

<!-- dax-check: measure -->
```
Margin % =
VAR Rev = [Revenue]
RETURN
    DIVIDE ( Rev - [Standard Cost], Rev )
```

In the formula bar, Shift+Enter starts a new line within a measure, and Enter commits it. Margin % is a ratio of totals, calculated anew for every cell, which no implicit measure could do.

**Step 4. Write the discount rate.** The rate is discount dollars divided by the dollars before discount, the ratio that Average of Discount misstated in Chapter 13.

a. Add the two measures below.
b. Format Discount Rate as a percentage with two decimals.

<!-- dax-check: measure -->
```
Price Before Discount =
SUMX ( SalesInvoiceLine, SalesInvoiceLine[Quantity] * SalesInvoiceLine[UnitPrice] )
```

<!-- dax-check: measure -->
```
Discount Rate = DIVIDE ( [Discounts], [Price Before Discount] )
```

Price Before Discount multiplies each line's quantity by its unit price, so the rate divides the discount dollars by the dollars they were taken from, and each line counts in proportion to its value. For fiscal 2026 the rate is well above the average of the Discount column that Chapter 13 found misleading, because the discounted lines are larger than the average line.

**Step 5. Use CALCULATE to fix one filter and remove another.**

a. Add the two measures below, and format Furniture Revenue as an amount and Share of Revenue as a percentage.
b. On a new page named `Margins`, add a table visual with ItemGroup from Item and the measures Revenue, Furniture Revenue, and Share of Revenue.
c. Add a slicer with Year from the Date table, and select 2026.

<!-- dax-check: measure -->
```
Furniture Revenue = CALCULATE ( [Revenue], 'Item'[ItemGroup] = "Furniture" )
```

<!-- dax-check: measure -->
```
Share of Revenue =
DIVIDE ( [Revenue], CALCULATE ( [Revenue], REMOVEFILTERS ( 'Item' ) ) )
```

Furniture Revenue shows the same amount on every row, because its filter replaces the row's item group. Share of Revenue gives each group's share of fiscal 2026, with Furniture holding more than half, because it removes the filter on Item but keeps the year.

**Step 6. Show Furniture's margin by quarter.**

a. Add a matrix with ItemGroup from Item on **Rows**, YearQuarter from Date on **Columns**, and Margin % as **Values**.
b. Filter the matrix to the years 2025 and 2026 in the **Filters on this visual** section.
c. Read the Furniture row across the eight quarters.

@fig-14-07 shows the matrix. Furniture's margin at standard cost holds steady through the first half of 2026, falls in the third quarter, and falls again in the fourth, to its lowest level in the two years, the decline the controller asked about in Part I. Each total is a margin of its own, calculated from the totals of revenue and cost, not an average of the cells beside it.

![Margin at Standard Cost by Item Group and Quarter.](/visuals/svg/fig-14-07-margin-matrix.svg){#fig-14-07 fig-alt="A mock of a Power BI matrix with the item groups as rows, the quarters of fiscal 2025 and 2026 as columns, and the margin percentage at standard cost in each cell, with a total row and a total column. The Furniture row is outlined: its margin moves within a narrow band from the first quarter of 2025 to the third quarter of 2026, and falls clearly below that band in the fourth quarter of 2026."}

**Step 7. Write the first test.** Each test is a query whose result must equal a total you already trust.

a. Select **DAX query view** in the bar on the left.
b. Double-click the query tab and rename it `Tests`.
c. Type the query below with its comment line, select it, and click **Run**.
d. Record the result.

<!-- dax-check: query -->
```
// Test 1: fiscal 2026 revenue and lines must equal Chapter 6's control totals
EVALUATE
SUMMARIZECOLUMNS (
    'Date'[Year],
    "Lines", [Invoice Lines],
    "Revenue", ROUND ( [Revenue], 2 ),
    "Gross Margin", ROUND ( [Gross Margin], 2 ),
    "Margin %", ROUND ( [Margin %], 4 )
)
ORDER BY 'Date'[Year]
```

The test rounds its amounts to the cent and its ratio to four decimals, because the results grid ignores the measures' formats. Its 2026 row should equal Chapter 6's invoice line count and line total, as in @fig-14-06.

**Step 8. Write the second test.**

a. Type the query below under the first, with its comment line.
b. Select it, and click **Run**.

<!-- dax-check: query -->
```
// Test 2: Furniture margin by quarter must equal the margins of Chapter 6's bridge
EVALUATE
SUMMARIZECOLUMNS (
    'Date'[YearQuarter],
    TREATAS ( { "Furniture" }, 'Item'[ItemGroup] ),
    TREATAS ( { 2026 }, 'Date'[Year] ),
    "Revenue", ROUND ( [Revenue], 2 ),
    "Gross Margin", ROUND ( [Gross Margin], 2 ),
    "Margin %", ROUND ( [Margin %], 4 )
)
```

TREATAS applies a list of values as a filter on a column, here Furniture and fiscal 2026. The result should show the Furniture margin of the third and fourth quarters that Chapter 6's bridge started from and ended at. A test that fails is a finding about the model, not about the business: look for a missing relationship, a filter that reached the wrong table, or a measure that summed what it should have iterated.

**Step 9. Document the measures.**

a. Select **Model view**, and select Revenue in the Measures table.
b. In the **Properties** pane, type a description, such as `Invoiced revenue: the sum of LineTotal on the invoice lines.`
c. Add a description to each of the other measures.
d. On the **Validation** page, add Invoices, Standard Cost, and Margin % to the table of totals, and save the report.

A reader who points at a measure in the Data pane now sees what it means, and the Validation page shows the new measures beside the control totals they must agree with.

**Checkpoint.** Your model should now pass these checks:

- The Measures table holds the sales measures, each with a format and a description, and appears at the top of the Data pane.
- Test 1's fiscal 2026 row equals Chapter 6's control totals, and Test 2 reproduces the Furniture margins at the two ends of Chapter 6's bridge.
- Discount Rate is higher than the Average of Discount of Chapter 13, and Share of Revenue adds up to 100% across the item groups of a year.

The measures now say what the report's numbers mean, and the tests prove it. The fall in Furniture's margin is visible quarter by quarter. Comparing it with the same quarter of the year before needs time intelligence, which the next section explains and Exercise 14.3 builds.
